title: Atoms, Chemical Bonds And Electromagnetic Radiation

sections.title: Atomic structure and the periodic system
sections.text:
An atom consists of a small nucleus containing protons and usually neutrons, surrounded by electrons described through quantum states. Protons are positive, electrons negative and neutrons electrically neutral. Most atomic mass is in the nucleus. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons; an ion has gained or lost electrons.

Atomic number $Z$ is proton number and identifies the element. Mass number $A$ is the total number of protons and neutrons, so neutron number is $A-Z$. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have six protons, but they have six and eight neutrons respectively. They are isotopes of carbon, not different elements. Some isotopes are stable and others radioactive.

Electrons occupy energy levels and orbitals rather than travelling on tiny fixed planetary tracks. The outer electron arrangement strongly influences bonding. Elements in the same periodic-table group often have related chemical properties because of similarities in valence electrons. Periods correspond broadly to changing electron-shell occupation across rows. Atomic mass on a periodic table is usually an isotopic average, not the mass number of every atom.

sections.title: Chemical bonding and material properties
sections.text:
Chemical bonds arise from electromagnetic interactions and the energy changes accompanying different electron arrangements. Ionic bonding involves electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions. Sodium chloride forms an extended crystal lattice; an individual “salt molecule” is not the most accurate description of the bulk crystal. Ionic solids are often brittle and can conduct electricity when molten or dissolved because ions can move.

Covalent bonding involves shared electron density between atoms. Molecules such as water have covalent bonds internally, but substances such as diamond form extensive covalent networks. Metallic bonding involves delocalized electrons in a solid structure, helping explain conductivity and malleability. These broad categories overlap in real materials.

| Interaction | Basic description | Example and implication |
|---|---|---|
| Ionic bond | Attraction between ions | Salt lattice; mobile ions in solution carry charge |
| Covalent bond | Shared electron density | Water molecules; carbon networks |
| Metallic bond | Delocalized electrons in metallic structure | Copper conducts electricity |
| Hydrogen bond | Directional attraction involving suitably bonded hydrogen | Helps organize water and biomolecules |

Intermolecular attractions influence boiling point, solubility and biological structure. Breaking water's intermolecular attractions during boiling does not normally split each molecule into hydrogen and oxygen. Polar water interacts well with many ions and polar molecules, whereas nonpolar oils do not mix readily with it. Chemical structure therefore links everyday observations with atomic behaviour.

sections.title: Reactions, acids and oxidation
sections.text:
A chemical reaction rearranges atoms and bonds. A balanced equation conserves each element's atoms and total electric charge; it does not require all products to have the same physical properties as the reactants. Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings; endothermic processes absorb it. A catalyst lowers an activation barrier and accelerates approach to equilibrium without changing the equilibrium constant at the same temperature.

Acids can donate protons in the Brønsted–Lowry description; bases accept them. For dilute aqueous solutions, $pH\approx-\log_{10}[H^+]$ when concentration approximates activity and is expressed relative to the standard concentration. A decrease of one pH unit corresponds approximately to ten times the hydrogen-ion activity. Neutral pH is about 7 at 25°C, with the neutral value changing with temperature. Strong acid and concentrated acid describe different properties: ionization behaviour and amount per volume.

Oxidation is electron loss and reduction electron gain. They occur together. Combustion, rusting, cellular respiration and many treatment processes involve redox chemistry. Oxidation need not always mean direct addition of molecular oxygen; electron transfer is the more general definition.

sections.title: Waves, photons and the spectrum
sections.text:
Electromagnetic waves involve coupled electric and magnetic fields and can travel through vacuum. Wavelength $\lambda$ is distance between corresponding wave points, frequency $f$ is cycles per second and vacuum speed satisfies $c=f\lambda$. Wavelength is in metres, frequency in hertz and $c$ in metres per second. A 100 MHz radio signal has wavelength approximately $3\times10^8/(100\times10^6)=3$ metres in vacuum.

Photon energy is $E=hf$, where $h$ is Planck's constant in joule seconds and $f$ is frequency in hertz. Higher frequency means greater energy per photon, while intensity also depends on how much radiation is present. Intense low-frequency radiation and a high-energy photon are different concepts.

From long to short wavelength, the spectrum includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. The boundaries are conventional. Infrared is useful in thermal imaging, visible light in ordinary vision, microwaves in radar and communication, and X-rays in diagnostic imaging. Many ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma-ray photons are ionizing; ordinary radio communication is non-ionizing. Non-ionizing radiation can still transfer energy, including heating at sufficiently high exposure. [NASA: electromagnetic spectrum](https://science.nasa.gov/ems/).

teaching.objective: Relate wavelength, frequency and photon energy, and calculate a wavelength with consistent units.
teaching.prerequisites: A cycle is one repetition. Hertz means cycles per second. A metre measures distance; mega means one million.
teaching.explanationHtml:
Radio waves and visible light belong to the electromagnetic spectrum. Frequency counts repetitions per second; wavelength measures the separation between corresponding points. In vacuum their product equals the speed of light.

Worked practice: use c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s. For 150 MHz, f = 150 × 10⁶ Hz and λ = c/f = 2 m. The units (m/s)/(1/s) leave metres. Doubling frequency at the same speed halves wavelength. Photon energy follows E = hf, so it doubles.

Try 75 MHz before checking: the wavelength is 4 m. Increasing intensity is a different change from increasing energy per photon. Compare these ideas with the original reference passage for the spectrum’s applications.
revision: c = fλ in vacuum; wavelength in metres, frequency in hertz.
E = hf; higher frequency gives higher energy per photon.
Convert MHz to Hz before calculating.

sections.title: Radioactivity and nuclear change
sections.text:
Radioactivity is spontaneous transformation of unstable nuclei. Alpha decay emits a helium nucleus; beta processes involve changes in nuclear proton–neutron composition and emission of appropriate particles; gamma radiation is high-energy electromagnetic emission from nuclear transitions. Different emissions have different penetration and ionizing behaviour, so shielding depends on the radiation and exposure pathway.

Half-life is the time required for half the radioactive nuclei in a large sample to decay statistically. After $n$ half-lives, $N=N_0(1/2)^n$, where $N_0$ and $N$ are initial and remaining nuclei. A hypothetical 80-unit sample becomes 40, 20 and 10 units after one, two and three half-lives. Decay does not mean a sample becomes instantly harmless at one half-life; remaining activity and daughter products matter.

Activity is measured in becquerels, one decay per second. Absorbed dose is measured in grays, joules per kilogram. Sieverts express radiation-protection quantities that account for biological weighting. These units answer different questions and cannot be substituted without the relevant physical and biological information.

**Ions, isotopes and reactivity.** Removing one electron from a neutral sodium atom produces a positive sodium ion without changing its element. Adding a neutron changes its isotope but not its proton number. A nuclear transformation that changes proton number creates a different element. These distinctions separate chemical processes, which mainly rearrange electrons and bonds, from nuclear processes that alter nuclei. An isotope can also retain broadly similar chemistry while differing in nuclear stability.

**Bond energy and reactions.** Breaking reactant bonds requires energy and forming product bonds releases energy. Whether the overall reaction releases or absorbs energy depends on the balance together with relevant thermodynamic conditions. A fuel does not contain miniature packets of heat waiting to escape: chemical energy differences become heat or useful work during a reaction pathway. Reaction rate is a separate issue, which is why a fuel and oxygen can coexist until a sufficient ignition process overcomes the activation barrier.

**Radiation pathways.** External exposure comes from a source outside the body; internal exposure follows inhalation, ingestion or another route of entry. A weakly penetrating alpha-emitting source can present a very different hazard when incorporated into tissue. Contamination means radioactive material is present where it is unwanted, while irradiation means exposure to radiation. An object exposed to X-rays is not thereby necessarily contaminated with a radioactive substance. These distinctions are central to interpreting environmental measurements and medical applications.

questions.prompt: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 atoms differ primarily in the number of:
questions.explanation: Both are carbon isotopes with six protons; carbon-12 has six neutrons and carbon-14 has eight.

supplementalQuestions.prompt: A radio wave in vacuum has frequency 150 MHz. With c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s, what is its wavelength?
supplementalQuestions.explanation: A: This is the reciprocal of the numerical answer and has no valid wavelength derivation. B: λ = c/f = (3 × 10⁸)/(150 × 10⁶) = 2 m. C: This has a power-of-ten conversion error. D: Multiplying speed by frequency gives the wrong units; wavelength requires division.

supplementalQuestions.prompt: A photon has twice the frequency of another photon. Which comparison is correct in vacuum?

options.A: Twice the wavelength and twice the energy
options.B: Half the wavelength and half the energy
options.C: Half the wavelength and twice the energy
options.D: The same wavelength and twice the energy

supplementalQuestions.explanation: A: Wavelength decreases when frequency increases at fixed speed. B: E = hf increases with frequency. C: c = fλ gives half the wavelength; E = hf gives twice the energy. D: Equal wavelengths at the same speed would require equal frequencies.

supplementalAnalytical.prompt: Explain how wavelength, frequency and photon energy are related. Calculate the wavelength of a 150 MHz wave in vacuum. (Original five-mark practice.)
supplementalAnalytical.answer_html: Wavelength is the distance between corresponding wave points; frequency is cycles per second. In vacuum c = fλ, so higher frequency means shorter wavelength. Photon energy E = hf increases with frequency. For f = 150 × 10⁶ Hz, λ ≈ (3 × 10⁸ m/s)/(150 × 10⁶ s⁻¹) = 2 m.

rubric.criterion: Define wavelength and frequency with units.
State c = fλ and the inverse relationship at fixed vacuum speed.
Use E = hf to explain photon energy.
Convert MHz to Hz and substitute into λ = c/f.
Give 2 m with units and suitable rounding.

commonMistakes: Multiplying c by f instead of dividing.
